Content: Jokes on you, I'm planning to pair a comparable GPU with a Ryzen 7 9800X3D. Why? Author: @King_Ears
Content:
It's not that bad. I'm hoping this will replace the 3050 that is in every budget pc in the UK. 

For context I purchased a pc for £500 last Christmas for my 11 yo son and as someone who hasn't been a pc gamer since the late 90s I had zero idea what was good etc, so I ended up just getting a cyberpower with Ryzen 5 4500, MSI 3050 8gb, 16 GB ddr4 2400mhz ram and 512 GB m.2 SSD. 

I have recently purchased a pc for myself to play iRacing and other racing Sims at high graphics settings and plumped for a 9800x3d and 5070ti pre built for £2k.

During my research I realised my son's pc specs are, well crap. However it plays everything he wants to play at 1080p high/mid graphics with no or very little frame drops. Roblox, beamNG, KSP, ravenfield, MSFS2020 and others all work surprisingly well considering the crappiness of the PC. 

So these GPUs definitely have a place in the world for low budget systems purchased by people (like myself at the time) who have no idea what they're buying and just want a PC for their kid that works with the majority of games they play without issues and doesn't cost more than a console. Kids like my son aren't bothered about 1440p or 4k. They just want a game that runs as smoothly as possible at 1080p and that's where the 5050 fits the bill.

Yes for people who will build their own system it's best to avoid, but this isn't aimed at DIYers imo.

Author: @ebridgewater
Content:
Current UK pricing (August 2025):

£216 Arc B580 (12GB GDDR6)
£218 RTX 5050 (8GB GDDR6)
£249 RTX 5060 (8GB GDDR7)
£260 9060 XT (8GB GDDR6)

I would say the RTX 5050 is an decent buy, considering the above 🤷🏻

The Arc B580's 12GVB VRAM is nice for the same price as the RTX 5050 but NVIDIA's software support is an important consideration.

Sure, you can get a faster card like the RTX 5060 but it is £30 more and the buyer may not have £30 more.

Plus, the RTX 5060 has been out a while so the price has dropped but the RTX 5050 is new - it will not be long before it is closer to £200 whereas the RTX 5060 will still hover around £250 for a while.

Author: @why_though
Content:
Makes sense when the only thing being considered is price/performance. But there are other important things that can sway the value proposition towards the 5050: longer software support than 4060 or 3060; better drivers than 580 ("DNF" is not something we should just be accepting); price/perf is a flawed metric, because performance improves exponentially over time, but comparisons are always made incorrectly as if it is linear (this is short sighted thereby not considering the entire PC lifetime and skewes the conclusion towars higher end models unfairly); 5050's new features and higher chance that new yet unanounced software features will be ported to it.

There is a lot being ignored in the comparison, at the very least I would disagree with making a generalised bad recommendation. It is a great card still. I know if i had to chose between 5050 3060 580 I'd actually chose the 5050 for my use case.

Author: @Alovon
Content:
To give some clarification tech-side and use case-wise about the 5050's characteristics vs the 4060, 3060-12GB. Or even the RX 9060s 
- It trading blows in raster is actually pretty impressive  considering it's 13TFLOPs vs 15TFLOPs (~15% more TFLOPs on the 4060). Although that is offset a bit by the 5050 having ~20% more memory bandwidth? It technically is one of the better gen-on-gen showcases for Blackwell in the desktop space (although tech-side stuff is only neat on-paper ofc)

- The RT performance results flipping back to the 4060 though is probably more becuase of a not-often spoken about reality to *how* NVIDIA's Architecture works WRT to RT...as in the RT cores outside of stuff like Path Tracing are tremendously overkill for most RT Calculations. The real cost being actually drawing the damn result in a fast enough manner on the Shader Cores lol. This is why NVIDIA made Ray Reconstruction as a thing becuase it offloads denoising from the Shaders into the Tensor cores and leaves more headroom to actually draw the rest of the image.
   - Fun fact about this characteristic of how NVIDIA's architectures work in RT. *Ampere*'s RT Cores are so cracked that in the Nintendo Switch 2 at 1.007GHz in its docked mode, they actually can spit out higher Ray-Intersect Testing values/rates than the whole PS5 if you devoted every CU to RT Acceleration (which would disable all the Texture Mapping units in the console so they never do that). Just for a reference to how OP the RT cores actually are and just how limited they are in Ray Tracing workloads by the Shaders.
   - So the 5050 lagging behind the 4060 in RT is probably becuase the 20SMs of Shaders are getting throttled width-wise relative to the 24SM (20% wider) 4060. Even if the 20 RT cores in the 5050 probably could spit out more RT Testing results than the 4060 in a time-window. Hypothetically a workload that is easier on the shaders at base (unlike Cyberpunk/Black Myth.etc), and then using Ray Reconstruction to also use the faster Tensor cores probably would flip results in favor of the 5050, but that's conjecture. 

- I will again point out how the VRAM demand "Problem" is sort of a echo of the technology-design transition (Standard Shading moving to Mesh Shading.etc) rather than a active one at this point beyond some outlier titles which just...aren't actually optimizing well on PC for memory usage? (*cough cough*, Indiana Jones and Doom The Dark Ages which have very-optimized Xbox Series S ports that typically run with 4GB of GPU memory) 90% of UE5 games that use UE5's features (Nanite, Lumen.etc) have VRAM usages that fit comfortably within a 8GB buffer even at 1440p (Clair Obscur). Games like Hogwarts Legacy, Jedi Survivor, The Last of Us Part 1/2, Indiana Jones/Doom The Dark Ages.etc are just games that poorly utilize/design their RAM setups whether it be via stressing legacy geometry pipelines to the limit (Howarts/Jedi), have a major case of engine tech-debt from the Texture Pool days and stubbornness on exposing console-level settings (the Idtech games), or sheer just bad coding/porting (TLOU), these are the outliers in all honesty. Not the standard. 
   - And extra note,  we really need to get developers who push out very good Xbox Series S conversions of their games to expose the freaking settings they use there on PC as like, WTF you got your game running and looking very good on a system with 8GB of unified memory split between the CPU/GPU in the 2020s, a system where the Nintendo Switch 2 has more memory than it, why aren't these options on PC. 

- On the note of the B580 and RX 9060 XT, NVIDIA's brand power and more importantly, ease of use are something I feel is greatly undervalued/ignored for the type of consumer considering these cards? The buyer looking at a budget GPU typically are ones trying to get into the PC space. So they don't know what a FSR4 is vs a FSR3 or the reasons why their GPU supports FSR4 but barely games have it VS FSR2/FSR3.etc. DLSS just *being* DLSS and having a lot more direct-integrations for DLSS4 makes it a lot easier to learn and explain to a user trying to get the most out of what may be their first Gaming PC. And DLSS's CNN model being better than anything outside of FSR4 or DLSS' own Transformer model helps too even if they aren't tech-savy enough to dig into the DLSS overrides (A major problem on AMD's side as most of the FSR4 "Support" is via very limited driver override toggles atm vs NVIDIA's comparatively far more open easy-use system). You can't expect a new consumer to learn what a Optiscaler is and mod FSR4 into all their games. 
  - I barely mentioned the B580 here in retrospect, that's primarily because Intel's route with XeSS has generally been better than AMD's with FSR4. Especially with them quickly walking back their XeSS 2 exclusivity meaning the status-quo of Arc cards having better behavior with XeSS by default is returned without leading into too much implementation weirdness. Although the B850 is bit more wishy-washy performance wise due to Intel's (a lot better mind) driver support woes still having some thorns in the side. 

- As a final note, yeah the 5060 is a far better GPU buy than the 5050 mind hah. 50$ is NOT a good enough saving versus the performance drop relative to it. And most of the points defending it are piggybacking off points that are generally beneficial to the 5060 which in the 5060's case it at least convincingly matches the next-tier up from it's last gen counterpart. If the 5050 was like, 200$ and targeted being a PCIE-power only 75W GPU it's proposition would be a lot better for it's performance. But as-is, yeeeaah.
